questions.question: What are named return values in Go, and when would you use them?
questions.title: Named Return Values
questions.direct_answer: Named returns declare the return variables IN the signature: func f() (result int, err error). They're initialized to zero, can be assigned throughout the function, and allow the naked return. Use for: documentation, defer modification, and clarity in multi-return functions.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Named returns declare the return variables IN the signature: func f() (result int, err error). They're initialized to zero, can be assigned throughout the function, and allow the naked return. Use for: documentation, defer modification, and clarity in multi-return functions.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The declaration:

```go
func split(sum int) (x, y int) {
    x = sum * 2 / 3   // assign directly — no :=
    y = sum - x
    return             // naked return — returns x and y
}

split(10)   // 6, 4 — executed
```

What named returns give, each with its moment:

1. Zero-initialized: x and y START at 0 — the signature declares and initializes. In a function building an error result gradually, `err` starts nil and is only set on failure — the failure paths return without explicitly naming err.

2. Naked return — return with no arguments returns the named values. Readability rule: naked returns are clear in SHORT functions (the split above); in long ones they hide which values are being returned — the community style is explicit returns except for short/obvious bodies.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    SIG[func f result int, err error] --> INIT[zero-initialized]
    INIT --> ASSIGN[assign through fn body]
    ASSIGN --> RET[naked return]
    DEFER[defer] --> CAN[can modify result before return]
```
